questions.question: Explain what terms of trade are, why they tend to deteriorate for primary-product exporters, and how this creates a trade imbalance between the developing and developed world.
questions.expected_answer: Terms of trade are the ratio of a country's average export prices to its average import prices — a measure of what its exports can buy. They improve when export prices rise faster than import prices and deteriorate when import prices outrun export prices, forcing the country to export ever more volume to afford the same imports. Primary exporters suffer long-run deterioration because raw materials face constant competition and substitution — anyone can grow the crop or mine the ore — while manufactured goods carry technology, patents and branding that protect their prices. So a country selling ore and buying machinery is like a farmer whose bag of oranges bought a phone last year but needs three bags this year: working harder and affording less through no fault of its own. This mechanism, not laziness or bad luck, underlies the structural trade imbalance between developing countries locked into primary exports and developed countries selling protected, value-added manufactures — and it explains why development strategy pushes beneficiation and manufactured exports rather than simply exporting more raw material.

questions.question: Discuss the impact of globalisation on development, giving at least two positive and two negative impacts with examples, and deliver a balanced verdict.
questions.expected_answer: Globalisation — the growing interconnection of economies driven by cheap container transport, instant communication and lower trade barriers — cuts both ways. Positives: it opens world markets to developing countries, as South African fruit, wine and vehicles on foreign shelves show; it carries investment, factories and technology into developing economies through TNCs; and it created hundreds of millions of manufacturing jobs, lifting East Asia out of poverty at historic speed while giving consumers cheaper goods. Negatives: the benefits concentrate in favoured locations, reproducing the core-periphery pattern; TNCs hold bargaining power over governments, extracting tax breaks and lax regulation, repatriating profits and threatening relocation — the race to the bottom; local infant industries can be destroyed by imports, as South Africa's clothing and textile sector was, shedding tens of thousands of jobs to cheaper Asian producers; and interconnection transmits shocks, with the 2008 financial crisis cutting South African exports and jobs within months of starting on Wall Street. Balanced verdict: globalisation is a powerful engine that pulls unevenly — countries with skills, infrastructure and bargaining power ride it, while those without can be run over by it.

questions.question: Critically examine export-led development, using the Asian Tigers as evidence for the strategy and at least three arguments that limit it as a universal recipe, ending with its relevance to South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Export-led development grows an economy by selling manufactured goods to world markets. South Korea's version began with cheap-labour textiles, banked the foreign exchange, reinvested deliberately in education and infrastructure, and climbed the value ladder through steel, ships and cars to semiconductors — from Ghana-level income in 1960 to developed-world status within two generations, with the state protecting infant industries and directing credit throughout. But the recipe has limits. It requires open, growing world markets, and if every country exports simultaneously the markets flood; the Tigers also climbed under favourable access and with few competitors on the bottom rungs, conditions later entrants such as today's climbers facing China's dominance cannot replicate. The early rungs carried heavy human costs — low wages, long hours and suppressed unions — and export economies are exposed first and hardest to external shocks like 2008, while East Asia's deferred environmental bill arrived as industrial smog. For South Africa, export-led elements exist — the motor industry programmes, fruit and wine, AGOA access — but the country climbs with obstacles the Tigers lacked: electricity insecurity, distance from major markets and skills shortages. The critical conclusion: export-led growth is a proven route but not a guaranteed one; it depends on preconditions — education, infrastructure, capable government — that are themselves developmental achievements.
